statements.impact_statement: No part of gift-exchange runs tar or handles tar archives.
No part of gift-exchange runs shadow's tools or keeps login records.
gift-exchange never calls the C library's glob function: Python's glob module is its own code, and nothing the product runs imports glob.
gift-exchange never runs apt, and apt-key, where the flaw is, isn't in the image.
No part of gift-exchange runs Perl.

gift-exchange doesn't use systemd: nothing in the product runs the programs that use systemd's libraries, and systemd's services aren't in the image. Exploiting it needs a local user in the container, which is outside the product's operation; the app also runs as an unprivileged user with no login shell, and the container's no-new-privileges setting stops setuid programs from raising privileges.

No part of gift-exchange runs chown or chgrp. Exploiting this needs a local user running them in the container, which is outside the product's operation; the app also runs as an unprivileged user with no login shell, and the container's no-new-privileges setting stops setuid programs from raising privileges.
gift-exchange never uses the C library's regular expressions: Python's re module is its own engine, and nothing the product runs imports regcomp or regexec.

This is a way round the stack protector, not a vulnerability on its own. It only helps an attacker who already has another, worse bug in the program, one that lets them write large amounts of data to its memory; that bug would be the vulnerability. glibc's developers don't treat this as a security issue.
The flaw only matters when someone runs ldd on untrusted programs, which ldd's own documentation warns against, and no part of gift-exchange runs ldd.

gift-exchange never parses terminal descriptions: its processes don't load ncurses's terminal library, which only CPython's interactive tools use, and nothing in the product runs the ncurses programs that compile or translate termcap entries.
The flaw is in the infocmp program, which no part of gift-exchange runs; the ncurses libraries the product loads don't contain it.
The flaw is in SQLite's zipfile extension. Debian's libsqlite3, which gift-exchange uses, doesn't include it, and gift-exchange never loads SQLite extensions.
gift-exchange never uses the C library's regular expressions: Python's re module is its own engine, and nothing the product runs imports regcomp or regexec.
gift-exchange has no C++ code: nothing in the product loads the C++ standard library, where the flaw is.

gift-exchange runs dash only for its start script, once when the container starts, with input only from the operator's configuration; the script does no pattern matching, so dash's vulnerable matcher never runs.

The only HTTP responses gift-exchange parses come from the email provider's API, over TLS verified against certifi's bundle, and from its own server, in the health check. Only the provider could send a malformed Content-Length, and it can already send any response it likes, so lenient parsing gives it nothing new; TLS rules out an intermediary that frames responses differently.
The flaw is in OpenSSL's CMS encryption, which gift-exchange never uses: nothing in the product calls CMS, and OpenSSL's TLS doesn't use it.

The flaw is in std::from_chars() in libstdc++, the C++ standard library. Nothing gift-exchange runs is C++ or loads libstdc++: in the image only apt and its libraries do, and nothing in the product runs apt.
The flaw is in the C library's wide scanf functions (swscanf and the like), which nothing gift-exchange runs calls; no program in the image calls them at all.
gift-exchange passes socket.getaddrinfo() only its email provider's API host and port, which come from Anymail or the operator's secret files. Nothing a user sends becomes a host name or port.

gift-exchange never runs SQL that anyone outside it writes, so no one can send SQLite the chain of thousands of common table expressions this needs, in a query or in a view in a database the app opens.
gift-exchange has no full-text tables and never runs SQL that anyone outside it writes, so SQLite's FTS3 snippet() code, where the flaw is, never runs.
gift-exchange has no full-text tables and never runs SQL that anyone outside it writes, so SQLite's FTS5 code, where the flaw is, never runs.

gift-exchange sets no SQLite authorizer, so there are no read restrictions to bypass, and it never runs SQL that anyone outside it writes.

Exploiting this needs an R-Tree table with a tampered shadow table, which only a crafted database or SQL of the attacker's choosing can create. The only database gift-exchange opens is its own, on a volume only the app writes, with no R-Tree tables, and it never runs SQL that anyone outside it writes.
gift-exchange never uses SQLite's session extension, where the flaw is: nothing it runs applies changesets.
gift-exchange never runs SQL that anyone outside it writes, so no one can send SQLite the count(*) over a huge multi-row VALUES clause this needs, in a query or in a view in a database the app opens.

The flaw is in how glibc's gettext reads the LANGUAGE variable, which it does only when a process's messages locale (LC_MESSAGES) is something other than C. gift-exchange's processes never set their messages locale from the environment, so it stays C whatever LANG, LC_ALL or LANGUAGE say, and gettext never reads LANGUAGE. Setting those variables also needs control of the processes' environment, which only the operator has.
The flaw is in OpenSSL's QUIC client, and gift-exchange doesn't use QUIC: its only use of Debian's OpenSSL is TLS over TCP, through CPython's ssl module, to send email.

The flaw is in OpenSSL's AES-GCM-SIV cipher, which gift-exchange never uses: TLS has no AES-GCM-SIV cipher suite, nothing else in the product calls a cipher in Debian's OpenSSL, and the app's own encryption (Fernet) is AES-CBC with HMAC, in cryptography's bundled OpenSSL.
The flaw is in dpkg-source, which unpacks Debian source packages, and dpkg-source isn't in gift-exchange's image: only the dpkg package is, which installs and queries binary packages.
